extracted.intended_audience: art-loving travelers, students of painting, and art critics visiting Venetian galleries
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for reading, judging, and appreciating Tintoretto's paintings (especially the Scuola di San Rocco and other Venetian works), with attention to color, composition, lighting, viewing distance, and fidelity to subject. Useful for visitors, critics, and students assessing works in situ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of reflective accessories to enhance effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Small accessories (jewels, armlets, wings) can contribute greatly to a picture's effect by giving play of color and hinting character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes that the 'lustre of the jewels in the armlet of the evil angel' and the 'beautiful colours of his wings' are slight accessories but 'enhance the value of all the rest' and serve as the only hint of the Tempter's real character; such details are to be enjoyed by the painter and noticed by the critic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drapery should contribute color and interest (not be 'mere drapery')
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of Sir Joshua's rule: 'that drapery is to be mere drapery, and not silk, nor satin, nor brocade.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ruskin argues this rule is unwise for works of colour: painters like Tintoretto need fur, velvet, jewels, armour, or rich stuffs to 'put play of colour into' figures. Evaluate whether drapery is treated as dead folds or as an opportunity for colour and texture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of subject to the painter's strengths
rubrics_metrics.description: Some subjects (e.g., hospital population, disgusting scenes) lack points of contrast and do not suit a great colourist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic advises not to spend time on pictures whose subjects (like a hospital scene) offer little contrast or delight; consider whether the subject allows the artist to deploy their strengths (colour, texture, light) effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of scale and detail for viewing distance
rubrics_metrics.description: Pictures painted for effect from below or from a distance are often broad and gain little by close examination; heads may be coarse when seen near.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the level of finish and head-size is appropriate for intended viewing distance. Works intended for distant effect should be judged by their effect in situ, not by close inspection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of colour to express narrative meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Colour arrangement and contrasts (warm shadow vs cool light; white or coloured garments) express story and meaning (e.g., Deity as giver of bread shown in snow white).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for deliberate colour choices that symbolise elements of the story (e.g., Moses's scene: black/red foreground vs bright gold/blue distance to suggest joy after sorrow). Colour relationships should contribute to narrative comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of composition: binding vs radiating (love of space)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two approaches to unity: binding compositions into knots (Rubens, Michelangelo) vs uniting by springing from one source and embracing space (Tintoretto).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the composition's unity arises from compact binding or from a radiating source and love of space; determine which approach better suits the subject and feels truthful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausibility/naturalism of invented monsters or details
rubrics_metrics.description: More believable, probable designs (small winged lamprey-like serpents) produce greater terror than grandiose but improbable inventions (huge boa-like serpents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge imaginative elements by their plausibility; 'veritableness' (a believable imagination) often makes grotesque creatures more awful and effective than monstrous exaggerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mastery of atmospheric and transparent light effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of sunbeams, mists, clouds, and transparent spheres (bubbles) to veil figures and create sublime effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for subtle tricks of transparent light (e.g., angel surrounded by a globe, sunbeams veiling faces) that enhance sublimity; praise work that perceives and uses distant atmospheric phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressiveness: faces versus gesture
rubrics_metrics.description: Some works rely little on expression in the human countenance, telling the story by gesture instead; this can be effective at distance but unsatisfactory up close.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging a painting, note whether the emotional content is carried by faces or gestures and whether that choice succeeds at the intended viewing scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation of a painter's energy across works (vigor vs fatigue)
rubrics_metrics.description: A painter who throws intense energy into some works may be languid or heavy in others; heaviness of colour can be a symptom of fatigue or later repainting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether a dullness or heaviness in colour indicates the artist's fatigue, later repairs, or a genuine stylistic choice; compare strong and weak works to judge consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colour vitality and restraint (avoid oppressive reds and browns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive heaviness in reds and hot hues can injure a composition; choice of prevailing hues should suit the subject (e.g., Valley of Dry Bones being largely red/brown is strange).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether colour choices invigorate the scene or create an oppressive tone inconsistent with the subject; watch for areas suffering from 'heaviness of colour' possibly due to overpainting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anatomical and physical truthfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Accurate, physically convincing depiction (e.g., arrows in St. Sebastian driven like lances rather than 'stuck like pins') enhances truth and impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the believability of wounds, gestures, and physical consequences portrayed. Detailed, realistic handling of physical facts strengthens immediacy and truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and complication of light and shade
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex and original arrangements of light and shade (cloud drift, contrasted masses) contribute to magnificence and interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise compositions whose grandeur comes from inventive handling of light and shadow rather than merely from individual figures; consider how cloud-drift and complicated lighting amplify the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artist's evident delight in the subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Paintings where the artist has evidently delighted (shown by vigorous, joyful handling) are superior to those done 'coldly' or as exhausted fulfilments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Try to detect a painter's pleasure or boredom in the handling; works done with delight often display stronger invention and stronger execution than 'dregs' or tired work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value and placement of decorative minor figures/elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Minor decorative pieces (children's heads, marbling, fruit) should not squander the artist's best qualities in mere vacuities; they should be worthwhile, not merely fillers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether decorative bits add beauty and interest or merely fill space; small decorative works can be very fine but should not be 'lost in filling small vacuities of the ceiling.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of display and lighting conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Some pictures are best seen under particular lighting (e.g., Christ before Pilate 'best seen on a dark day' when the white figure reads like a spirit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If possible, assess paintings in the lighting conditions in which they are intended to be seen; lighting can radically alter perceived success and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retain characteristic style rather than unsafe imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Departing from one's own manner to imitate another (e.g., Tintoretto attempting Correggio-like brightness) risks losing one's virtues without gaining the imitator's strengths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether a work retains the artist's characteristic strengths; be critical of 'showy' departures that lack the master's deeper virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolic use of colour for attributes and roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific colour treatments of figures (e.g., Supreme Being in white to signify giver of bread; elsewhere red and blue) should be read symbolically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for consistent symbolic uses of colour for figures and roles; note how colour choices help convey theological or narrative meanings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of atmospheric cloud and veil for sublimity
rubrics_metrics.description: Transparent veils of cloud can veil faces and forms, producing delicate and sublime effects when handled well (contrast with rotund studio clouds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe how clouds are formed—whether they are noble, transparent, and veiling in a way that enhances the subject, or merely studio rotundities that detract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Background narrative elements enrich the principal scene
rubrics_metrics.description: Inserting narrative details in the distance (tents, battles) can expand the story and give depth to the principal action (e.g., Moses scene showing Amalek in distance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how background elements support and amplify the central story; good multi-planar storytelling in the background is praised as 'exquisite expression by mere colour.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion and compositional balance of dominant elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Oversized or oddly proportioned elements (e.g., Jonah's whale and an excessively large tongue) unbalance composition and may appear careless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the scale of major motifs fits the composition and the viewer's expectation; disproportion can distract unless intentionally expressive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fidelity to textual/scriptural detail where relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Accurate adherence to scriptural details (e.g., Abraham 'set the wood in order') matters; deviations that reflect carelessness may be criticized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When paintings depict known texts, compare the visual narrative to the source; deliberate departures may be artistic choices, but careless inaccuracies can be faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of finish and quality across a work
rubrics_metrics.description: Some elements may be 'tired work' or 'slovenly' while others are sublime; overall value depends on consistency of execution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate both the major compositions and the smaller bits (figures between windows, marbling); inconsistency suggests fatigue or uneven attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalness of gesture vs affected theatricality
rubrics_metrics.description: Affected, overstrained gestures (e.g., a scribe lifting his hand to dip a pen in an over-passionate way) detract from truthfulness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer gestures that feel natural and appropriate to the action; avoid theatrical poses that call attention to themselves rather than to the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of transcendent or ineffable quality (sublimity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some paintings (e.g., the Crucifixion) may be 'beyond all analysis' and possess an intensity that defies metric evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge when a work's power is primarily emotive and transcends analytic criteria; such works demand allowance for ineffable effect in any judgment.
